analysis.one_liner: Bans health insurers from turning down sick customers or charging them more, and requires open pricing.
analysis.headline: Referred to three House committees the day it was introduced, the bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote and died when that Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have banned preexisting-condition exclusions in every employer health plan and every individual insurance policy, and required insurers to sell coverage to anyone lawfully in the United States who applied. Each insurer would have to charge the same premium for the same policy within a geographic area — in both the group and individual markets — disclose those prices publicly, including online, and accept every employer that applied for group coverage. The Health and Human Services Secretary would write rules to discourage people from waiting until they got sick to buy insurance.
analysis.who_benefits: People with preexisting conditions, who at the time could be rejected outright or priced out of individual coverage; people who buy insurance on their own rather than through work; workers whose HMO plans imposed waiting periods before coverage started; employers of any size whose group included a costly illness and could be declined; and lawfully present immigrants, who would get the same guaranteed access as citizens.

how_it_helps.text: Bans preexisting-condition exclusions in every group health plan and every individual insurance policy, under ERISA, the tax code, and the Public Health Service Act.

Requires insurers selling individual coverage to accept any eligible applicant — citizens, lawful permanent residents, and other lawfully present immigrants — and bars them from declining or delaying that person's enrollment.

Requires every insurer to charge the same premium for the same policy within a geographic area, in both the group and individual markets, and to disclose those prices openly, including on the internet.

Extends guaranteed availability so insurers must accept every employer that applies for group coverage, not just small employers, so a workforce that includes a costly illness can no longer get a whole company turned down.
Removes the statutory option that let nonfederal governmental plans opt out of these group-market requirements, and bars HMO waiting periods before group coverage starts.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers, which would lose health-based screening and pricing — the tools for keeping premiums lower for healthy customers — and, because the bill includes no coverage mandate or subsidies, healthier policyholders, who would likely pay higher premiums to cover guaranteed-issue enrollees.

drawbacks.text: Guaranteed issue with no requirement to carry insurance invites people to wait until they are sick to buy coverage, which can push premiums up for everyone in the individual market. The bill responds only by letting the Health Secretary write rules to deter late enrollment, not by building a firm enforcement mechanism.

Uniform premiums mean people in good health pay more than their own expected costs so that people with illnesses pay less — a deliberate redistribution whose size would depend on rules the Secretary wrote later.

The bill creates no subsidies and no obligation to buy coverage, so a guaranteed offer could still be unaffordable: many people denied insurance at the time would have been offered a policy they could not necessarily pay for.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections are sound — and they are essentially what Congress enacted a year later in the Affordable Care Act, where they were paired with an individual mandate and subsidies that this bill lacked, the pieces that keep guaranteed-issue markets stable. Standing alone, the bill risked pushing individual-market premiums upward as healthy people delayed buying; its answer was only discretionary anti-gaming rules from the Health Secretary, not a firm mechanism. Group plans, which had carried partial portability protections since the 1996 HIPAA law, gained the most at the least risk. On balance the protections outweigh the costs, but the design was incomplete.

outcome.mechanism: It went to three House committees the day it was introduced and never came out of any of them; no committee or floor vote was ever held, and it died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011 — though its central protections became law anyway the following year in the Affordable Care Act.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Kagen, a Wisconsin Democrat, introduced the bill on February 13, 2009.
The same day, it was referred to three committees — Energy and Commerce, Education and Labor, and Ways and Means — with the Speaker to divide its provisions among them.
It was sent to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee on February 23, 2009, and to the Education and Labor Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions on March 30, 2009.
No further action was ever recorded — no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote.
The bill ended the Congress with 6 cosponsors, all Democrats, and none of the three referred committees ever voted on it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers kept health-based underwriting in the short run, but patients did not lose the substance: Congress wrote guaranteed issue, the preexisting-condition ban, and uniform rating into law the following year in the Affordable Care Act — paired with a coverage mandate and subsidies that brought insurers millions of new customers, terms this bill alone did not offer.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers, until the ACA enacted it with subsidies

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no recorded opposition exists; all support on the record came from Democrats — the sponsor plus 6 of 253 House Democrats as cosponsors, with no Republicans.

industries.note: The bill strips insurers' core risk-selection tools: no declining sick applicants, no preexisting-condition exclusions, no pricing the same policy differently by health status in the group or individual market, and no HMO affiliation waiting periods. It contains no coverage mandate or subsidies to bring in healthy customers, so insurers would absorb the cost of guaranteeing issue without an offset.

Insurers would have to accept every employer that applied for group coverage — not just small employers — so a firm whose workforce included someone costly could no longer be turned down, protecting its employees' access to coverage.
State and local government plans would lose their statutory option to opt out of certain group-market requirements, though their employees would gain the same standard protections other workers have.
